1. The animation shows inflation eroding the buying power of a fixed income payment. A retiree named Ruth gets a check. Her first check buys 10 crates of goods. The label says this is US consumer prices (CPI-U), illustrative, history and not a forecast.

2. The number of crates the check can buy changes over time. In the first frames, a row of about 10 crates sits next to the check. In the later frames, the last crate goes dark, and the check is labeled "+2% a year." A bracket then marks "today: about 9 in 10 crates (90.4%)," so the same check buys about 9 crates instead of 10.

3. It means that a check that is the same size, or that grows more slowly than prices, buys less as time passes. Even with a 2% yearly raise, the check's purchasing power ended up slightly lower, at 90.4% of what it was at the start. So the check rose in dollars but fell in real value.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that prices rise over time and that a payout that is fixed or rises by a set percentage may not keep up with inflation. For someone comparing two annuity payout options, they might look closely at whether a payout adjusts for inflation. They would also want to compare how much less the inflation-adjusted option pays at the start. This is my reading and not something the video states.

5. The advice in 4 is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the history of US prices and the shrinking crate count, and it labels itself as illustrative and "not a forecast." It doesn't recommend either payout option. The picture also doesn't say which of the two options the quote's "+2% a year" check matches.
